en: The Śrī-Śrī-Gopāla-Campū:
The Later Campū; now, the first supplement.
Obeisances to Śrī Śrī Rādhā-Kṛṣṇa. Auspicious Invocation: O Śrī Kṛṣṇa Caitanya, who possesses the form of Sanātana!
O Gopāla, O Raghunātha, O Lord of Vraja obtained by [the grace of] Āpta, protect me!
Since this Gopālacampū was previously completed quickly by relying on them alone,
therefore this subsequent [portion] shall also be superior.
Thus, O Lord, whom else but You should we worship? [Svāgatā meter] [1] Now, in due order, the ancient narrative shall be recounted:
[2] There is, it is said, a forest named Vṛndāvana, which encompasses the entirety of Vṛndāvana.
[3] Wherein it is like the circle of luminaries in the sky,
like the Dharma in the possessor of the Dharma,
and like the determination of reality in the Veda.
Like happiness upon the attainment of what is desired, like aesthetic flavor within the group of excitants and so forth, like the sixfold policy within the self;
Like one's own self in one's own love,
and like Nārāyaṇa in the supreme ether,
that Kṛṣ� thirsting people experience Him as their own refuge.
It accepts its own status as a refuge;
and therein they recognize the realm named Goloka, which exists beyond the light accessible to people such as ourselves through the science of invisibility.
And in that Goloka, Keśava—whose every slight thought is like a wish-fulfilling gem—[resides for] those inhabitants who shine with all-encompassing bliss.
Not abandoning the calamity of the accumulation of conceptual proliferation that uproots the attainment of the fifth human goal known as love (*prema*),
he manifests himself appropriately as a son and so forth solely under its influence, never deviating from it anywhere.
And having emerged from that very state, shining incomparably together with them in his loveliness, he— who is indeed the destroyer of the wicked— sometimes even intoxicates this world.
Then, like a leader of divine dancers entering from the dressing room, he likewise enters there.

Such being the case, following the account of the battle involving Vāñchita, Sadanta, Vakradanta, and Dantavakra, when his entry into that region occurred— characterized by the dimensions and marks to be described hereafter—
[he entered].

Then, on one occasion, two young princes named Madhukaṇṭha and Snigdhakaṇṭha— the sons of Sūta, who were experts in the stainless science of devotion to Hari, who had reached the further shore of all desires, and who had obtained the essence of that very association through the waves of the ocean of Śrī Nārada’s mercy— arrived at that same abode, which was graced by the illustrious Lord of Vraja and his sons.

Then, surrounding that practice of their conduct and being devoted solely to it, those two noble youths— resembling musical instruments bound by strings— frequently engaged in conversation with one another regarding the nature of things and even their doubts, and thus they brought forth the narrations of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s pastimes in Vraja, which are the very essence of all happiness.

[8] And there, they performed for him the ancestral conduct of his father and grandfather; performing that former conduct, they acted as if they were enacting a new poem consisting of the excellence of his life's deeds, and by means of their own life-conduct, they made it as if it were his very birth-conduct. [9] And immediately thereafter, they described his various exploits in their proper sequence.
[10] This is recalled here for the purpose of expanding upon the subsequent discourse: "Aha!
By whom indeed Pūtanā became a female demon (pūtanārī), by him the cart fell due to its lightness, like a mere wicker-work."
Tṛṇāvarta became one whose limbs were shattered like a blade of grass (*tṛṇāvarta*),
while the pair of Arjunas received grace and became like Arjuna himself. Therein, Vatsaka was indeed a protector of calves (*vatsaka*).
But a crane must indeed be a crane;
and space ought to remain as space.
Let this matter rest for now.
But this is truly marvelous therein:
that even Agha was sinless,
and Kāliya, like a snake that has cast off its skin, is designated as "liberated" (nirmukta) while still living.

[13] Thus, even though he was possessed of supreme vigor, by virtue of his humility he blended his own fame with that of his elder; and because he caused Dhenuka and Pralamba to hang in the flames of the fire of their own prowess, this man— who has established himself in the practice of sweet conduct— attains the very essence of transformation within my heart.
[14] Oh! Behold the heart-warming affection he shows toward his own people—he who indeed made even the forest fire his own food for their sake.
[15] Although still a child according to the count of years, by virtue of his unimpaired limbs, he wielded the mountain as a parasol over his left arm like a fierce staff.
O friend! Observe also his profound curiosity,
he who has fashioned Sudarśana as truly Sudarśana, even though he had already attained the state of being Kudarśana.

Thinking, "It would indeed be improper for this one named Śaṅkhacūḍa to possess a crest-jewel (maṇicūḍatā)," he— as if acting as a Yakṣa— stole the crest-jewel from that Yakṣa-wealth (yakṣavitta) who was reduced to nothing but his conch-shell; he turned misfortune into fortune, and having drawn Keśin’s confidence toward himself and having drawn his own sense of fulfillment from that purpose, he manifested his possession of hair (keśavatā).
Moreover: whatever splendor of birth was produced, whatever beauty of childhood,
whatever radiance of youth, and whatever glory of adolescence belonged to the Enemy of Evil;
That same single [arrow] then suddenly stole our hearts; now, however, those very arrows have joined together and violently agitate us out of greed.
Remembering again and again my father’s and mother’s affection during my early years,
my friendship with those many companions during my boyhood, and the indescribable beauty of fresh youth in those fawn-eyed maidens,
my mind does not move forward, but rather turns back toward them once more.
"Let them come together and go far away, like merchants discovering a treasure within their own house.
(Gītā 2.1.4) Even so, we reflect upon this by weighing it against the other effort undertaken for its nourishment;
for although in various places those two sons of the charioteer manifested their respective qualities—the former his preeminence in delusion and the latter his sweetness—according to their nature.
Nevertheless, following the principle that "enjoyment does not reach full maturity without separation," they have described, in summary, how Śrī Kṛṣṇa— ever thirsting for Vraja—

engaged in dialogue with Śrī Nārada, who is expert in removing the heavy burden of suffering from His devotees, and subsequently related His journey to the city of the Yadus, His return to Vraja, and His union with the abode of Goloka.

[17] Having set aside all those various descriptions, when an opportunity arose on another day, the Lord of Vraja, accompanied by the people of Vraja, appeared in the assembly hall presided over by Śrī Kṛṣṇa during the forenoon; as before, they questioned those two (Nārada and Maitreya) regarding the details of His departure and other matters.
For this reason:
even though that which causes internal pain might appear to be so upon hearing of one's own continuous suffering, human beings nevertheless do not abandon it.
Even though the wound has reached a state of dryness, by the power of remembering you, it forcibly causes me to experience again and again that intense suffering which was previously felt.
Or rather—

when a kinsman is found after a long time, even though there is unhappiness on all sides, it does not pass away; for at that moment, the beloved one would not take him by the neck and lament if he did not do so.
But the people of Vraja, being ever modest, did not do this themselves;
rather, Kṛṣṇa recounted it to them through those two storytellers in the assembly.
[18] Then, having been questioned and touched by both pleasure and pain, those two praised [him] in this assembly of Śrī Kṛṣṇacandra, just as Kuśa and Lava did in the assembly of Śrī Rāmacandra.
There, first of all, Snigdhakaṇṭha spoke with longing.
[19] And therein is the auspicious invocation:
We follow the Goddess of Speech,
who is the Bhāgavata, the essence of all the Vedas, through whose aesthetic flavor and established doctrine [we find fulfillment].
Even a new poetic work attains the status of a valid means of knowledge.
[20] Then, recollecting the former *campū*, that Vraja rejoiced day by day; and Kṛṣṇa, being dark-complexioned, rejoiced greatly with Vraja, and Vraja with him.
Just as the moonlight is [enhanced] by the bright fortnight known as *sitā*, so too is the white radiance [of the Buddha] by the bright fortnight known as *sitā*.
[21] Thus, even in this case—
whether it be "his craving was black" (*kṛṣṇā āsīt tasya tṛṣṇā*) or "the craving was black for him" (*tṛṣṇāyai vā kṛṣṇaḥ*)— there is a distinction here.
The wise do not cite as an example in this regard a person who is endowed with his own inherent nature (*svaprakṛti*). (2.1.9)
Just as water is for the thirsty, food for those overcome by hunger, coolness for those scorched by heat, and a mass of warmth for those whose hearts are chilled by frost—
so too was Kṛṣṇa born for the people of Gokula.
At that time, he indeed returned to his state of busyness for the sake of the happiness of all people.

My father, that group of brothers, all those headed by sisters, husbands, and sons-in-law, my mother, the mother of my mother and father, the women headed by my paternal aunts, and likewise all others—
dwelling within the hearts of all of them simultaneously, and causing them to dwell [within me].
Within his heart, Kṛṣṇa made them manifest as if they were the very words proclaimed by the Vāsudeva-scriptures.
How could he not be one whose bodily splendor is honored by the jewels of the Lord of the Gods, whose eyes captivate the essence of the autumnal crane,
and who possesses the range of all intelligence?
He is the foremost among those who possess the sweetness of the happiness of a father and a mother.
In meditation they are like tortoises; in gazing, like partridges; in perceiving fragrance, like cows;
and in nourishing him with touch, these two Queens of Vraja are ever like birds—those who have long nurtured this hope that rises with ever-increasing longing.
Having attained it in their youth, they joyfully reached a state of profound maturity.
Observing his own true brotherhood in him, Rāma’s body blossomed day by day;
but how could he possibly diminish the remaining measure of Śeṣa’s own slenderness?
People, desiring their own welfare, have accepted this view according to the prescribed order.
Just as the primary vital breath and its various divisions relate to one and the same single Self, so too do Kṛṣṇa and Śrīla-dāma and the others eternally relate to that One.
Whatever task they have, they go to perform it.
For those servants who have become worthy of service by Lord Hari, He has become the very embodiment of their life-breath, sharing the likeness of their bodies;
they do not exist without Him, nor does He exist without them.
"His own [nature] has remained there"—this is seen as an illustration among those things by the wise. (2.1.16)
If the cow-pen, the forest, and so forth should offer a fragrance that delights the sense of smell,
then there would be a row of white [cows] therein.
The earth was instantly awakened, but not at any other time.

If one would not believe that the world is [transformed] by his virtues, yet there are beings who are worthy of praise and who quickly become followers of one another, even those who were previously enemies;
if this is so, then the Blessed One himself, the illustrious son of Vyāsa, [is the witness].
One should not place before oneself the diamond-like inscriptions known as the Śrīmad-Bhāgavata.
Although every kind of happiness arose in the cowherd settlement, fear repeatedly arose from Kamsa’s own soldiers sent there to persecute Acyuta; therefore,
realizing that this was not a night of peace, he [Nanda] concluded this pastime.
In this world, the mind incessantly seeks to express its fear of the ascetic practices (dhūta).
[21] Then, as he was remembering that suffering, she spoke words of consolation to the Lord of Vraja, concluding her speech:
"This maker of sorrow and disease in the cow-pen, this ornament of your family, has come before you once again, shaking off all suspicion. (GC 2.1.20) Thus.
[22] Thus, this morning discourse was delivered within the assembly of the illustrious Lord of Vraja;

in that assembly, by taking their seats in a secluded spot, the illustrious Queen of Vraja and others, as well as Śrī Rādhā and the rest, each applied their ear to the description of the colors [of the Lord] that had been brought near to them.
[23] Then, as before, in a lovely and solitary place, the Lord of the Night (the Moon) shone within the night of Śrī Rādhikā—that which is most dear to the illustrious Beloved.
He attained a reunion that was the conclusion of their conversation;
and there Snigdhakaṇṭha said:
"Even Lakṣmī herself, though she has entered the heart of Acyuta, does so in another form."

Who can describe how much bliss the multitude of beautiful women of Vraja found by attaining this Govinda— who had been sought through austerities performed elsewhere but was not obtained in the splendor of the Rāsa dance and other pastimes— once he was brought under their control? //GC_2.1.21//
The Śrī-gopīs bestowed upon him that very grace which even Lakṣmī did not obtain, even in her dreams, during the splendor of the rāsa dance and other pastimes;
oh, how her fortune was such that it could not be grasped even by their longing!
"Can a poet describe the bliss that consists of that Rādhā?
[25] Then, having become heated for a moment and remaining silent, he spoke again: "Nevertheless, brother Madhukaṇṭha, the power to repeat this aloud once more does not manifest within me; for,"
Although the noble are surrounded by the praiseworthy people born of their own lineage, and although the conduct of the virtuous is indeed truly unswerving,
nevertheless, their practice of various high-flown deviations has utterly destroyed everything.
The pain of longing for Mukunda spreads delusion within my heart.
[26] Again, gazing upon the tearful face of Śrī Rādhā, he said:
"Her body is like a cluster of sun-gems touching the rays of the sun; her presence is like a multitude of moonstones touched by the luster of the moon."
Alas, that flame of Murāri’s, which even carries liquid, has become such that it causes my mind to whirl from every direction.
[27] Thus, repeating the same sequence, he spoke again regarding those various objects as follows:
"When Hari somehow came into their sight, at that time he produced a supreme flash of manifestation within them, but not as before."
Even when he has reached physical contact with me somewhere, that very distraction of his, like before, violently rends my heart.
This very distraction [of the mind] becomes far removed from the daughter of the Sun (Yamunā) upon attaining her; for when she laughs in secret, or even when she weeps,
then at her laughter, everything within him throbs and he rejoices exceedingly.
Likewise, O Lord, even this entire world experiences extreme exhaustion when You weep.
When the pastimes of Hari, beginning with the bliss of the Rāsa dance, were beautifully performed,
then the gopīs truly attained the highest of supreme happiness;
yet, they experienced a constant coming and going on all sides born of separation from Him.
Great suffering repeatedly crushes their hearts for us.
Because He, full of affection, cherished Rādhā— who stands supreme above all beloved ones— in His own heart with an uncommon love,
all this happiness of ours has vanished; alas, O Lord, O Beloved!
There he drinks with only a few verses; what shall I say, and what shall I do?

Remembering this again and again, my intellect burns with the thought that the love of the shy deer-eyed women of Vraja for Hari attained its full manifestation; let that suffice, for it was as if it were the very likeness of Rādhā herself, acting as the cause of its own radiance.
The crookedness in the vision [of the self] that seeks to perceive that [self] through valid cognition causes me distress.
That multitude of fair-browed cowherd girls who constantly sees Kṛṣṇa elsewhere, speaks of Kṛṣṇa through the words of others, and hears of Kṛṣṇa through what they hear—
alas, how could there be any intensity of concealment in them when [Kṛṣṇa] is clearly manifest?
Even for one such as she, the dullness of Rādhā would not have attained such intensity.
[28] Now, a similar statement should also be made regarding the beloved of the cowherd women:
"Prosperity shines under his control, and under his control is a succession of happiness;
since Kṛṣṇa subdues millions of goddesses of fortune, he clearly deserves millions of them. (GC 2.1.31)
Nevertheless, due to the power of the particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of divine play (*līlā*), even though they appeared otherwise at that time, those who were present perceived them as follows:
"He followed his beloveds, manifesting withering in their withering and radiance in their radiance."
This very [Self] is perceived by those who know the inner,
like the possessor of functions among the functions themselves.
O enemy of Mura, due to his profundity, emaciation and the like do not manifest clearly, as in the case of the ocean; rather,
it is because of his life-force that follows upon that [profundity].
Therefore, that [object] would be inferred by means of those mental streams.
Although Hari did not attain mastery over them upon their acquisition, nevertheless,
he possessed self-conceit regarding himself.
He considered his purpose to have been eternally fulfilled by his mother alone.
Let alone the going forth of the fair-browed women of Vraja,
their meeting at the rendezvous, and so on—
even their staying there of their own accord.
When understood, it produces joy toward Kṛṣṇa.
Like one who has been robbed of his own fortune by Bali, Kṛṣṇa went constantly to obtain them, which were ever being cut away, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
And among them, they thought of Rādhā most intensely.
A single blink of an eye might become an eon, and likewise, the ocean of tears from their eyes might become a kalpa; yet the beautiful women of Vraja continue to gaze at Hari.
Is it that such a state of being has come upon them, or rather, is it he who acts toward them in such a way?
Therefore, neither of these two—“these” nor “those”—admits of a definitive conclusion.

"Is this a visionary manifestation of that woman who caused my eyes to close, or is it her direct presence?"— thus Hari’s mind, incapable of discernment, his body encircled by the flames of its own internal longing, wandered powerfully toward some unknown place.
With his limbs fully blossomed, he at times experienced a soaring agitation every moment.
[30] Thus, that which has been described as being swallowed by suffering in whatever manner possible, and that other which is brought closer for description even more intensely than this—
it will indeed lead to the attainment of the supreme state of happiness in the ultimate future.
Just as one who wishes to travel through marshlands must leap over difficult terrain when facing impassable wells and desert lands,
so too it cannot be said that he will succeed merely by describing it;
look, look!
This very thing is now being accomplished in the contemplation of the unimpeded union of Rādhā and Mādhava;
for it is precisely through this that whatever can be described may be described.

And that description is as follows: thus, along with the ascent to the state of *mahābhāva* produced by the delusion [of the world] on the part of Kṛṣṇa and the beloveds of Kṛṣṇa, their full youth has also swiftly arrived.

Therein, the lotus of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s face— which was born from the milk-ocean of the illustrious Lord of the Gopas, white with His sublime fame, embraced by the shimmering luster of His dark complexion, and which dispels the darkness with the light of His long eyes— [is described].

I worship Govinda, who is like the moon, whose luster is the life of the cakora birds that are the eyes of the gopīs, who is the source for the movement of desire, and who is filled with the nectar of youth and possesses imperishable digits.
[34] Of them, it was thus: the radiance of their moon-like faces with their fully blossomed lotus-eyes, their cheeks turning pale,
and their chests resplendent with rows of unblown buds of the thousand-petaled lotuses born thereon;
The youthful state of Śrī Hari’s cowherd mistress, who possesses the beauty of a riverbank with her fresh and praiseworthy rounded hips, has spread through the eyes like moonlight.

[35] Thus, while the fame of both— the moon of nectar-like supreme passion in the ocean of fresh youth, whose hands were abundantly filled for one another— was spreading everywhere, Garga, it is said, manifested that very thing which he had previously indicated for the purpose of removing Kṛṣṇa’s marriage with them.
He moved through that very world, which was agitated by the fear of being deprived of him;
[he thought: "If there were physical contact with Kṛṣṇa for these women, then all of Gokula would immediately become distressed by separation from him.
And so, at the word of Garga, her mother, father, and others made Kṛṣṇa grant them a boon that would destroy all obstacles.
And there, where Yogamāyā herself was personally honoring Kṛṣṇa, she performed austerities under the name Pūrṇimā for the sake of concealing her own identity;
becoming submissive through her arduous penance and seeing no other way out, she brought about their marriage elsewhere as a mere semblance of falsehood,
by means of a widespread practice characterized primarily by sleeplessness and vigilance, even though it involved no small amount of dream-like imagination everywhere.
In the same way, He brought about both the union with the limbs of those who appeared to be their husbands and their subsequent destruction;
for indeed, they did not feel resentment toward Kṛṣṇa, as shown by Śrī Śuka following the manner of the verse beginning with *nāsūyan khalu kṛṣṇāya* (BhP 10.33.37).
Thus has the direction been pointed out by Śrī Śuka, just as it was by Śuka.

[39] This being so, he and they, through the intense attraction produced by supreme longing and through their concealment, somehow brought about a great joy of mutual union that had been long accumulated.

[40] Then, according to the manner previously described, as their great passion gradually became known among those present, the elders— fearing on account of their minds a future union with Kṛṣṇa, and on account of their speech the scandal of the women's departure for the forest— [acted].

When the emanation had ceased and the awakening was merging, the younger brother of Balarāma— known by the name Madhumangala, who follows the twice-born Kṛṣṇa out of affection as His dear companion— joined that conversation and asked: "How is it that many days are seen to have passed since the news of Rādhā and the others' arrival?"
[41] Madhumangala said: "The very obstruction of many elders becomes the primary cause for that matter to come within the scope of awareness.
[42] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Oh!
Even that secret conduct—was it reported to the ears of the elders?"
[43] Madhumangala said: In that mental transformation, neither internally nor externally does knowledge flash forth.
Even for a single one of them there would be no manifestation; how much less so for those of such a kind?
[44] Śrī Kṛṣ�na said: Previously, even when they had reached the bloom of fresh youth, there was already great difficulty in entering among them due to their elders' restrictions;
how much more so now?
[45] Madhumangala said: Although this matter, which is contrary to pleasure, does not easily emerge from our mouths as something pleasant, yet...
Nevertheless, it shall be made the subject of this discourse simply because of the fame of your question.
And thus, I have indeed heard this well-known [verse] regarding those who give verbal abuse to virtuous women:
"Why do you brood? Alas, why do you sigh? Why do you look about the paths?"
"Why do you gaze at her friend's face here? Why do you sprinkle her breasts with the water from your eyes?
Why do you fall into such deep fainting? And why do you repeatedly mutter the two syllables 'Kṛṣṇa' while extending your horripilation and trembling? (Gītagovinda 2.1.42) Thus it is said.
[46] Now, let the conduct of the words and the description of the directions spoken by each of those sisters-in-law to their respective mothers regarding their distress be heard:

"The paths of my eyes were occupied by the virtuous matrons of the family, the range of my hearing by their conversation, and the passage of my nostrils by the arrangement of many fragrant incenses offered by me."
"O Mother, by what effort could that state of hers, which is entirely dark, ever become obscured in her mind? Why then do you vainly fly into a rage against me?

[47] Having heard this being described, she observed for a moment his withered complexion, and then, in order to pursue further details regarding this matter, she dispatched Madhumangala and fell into deep reflection.
Having entered within, he reflected:
"My teachers have brought this clamor of the people to my experience; likely my most illustrious fathers will lend their ears to it there."
"Then who indeed will remove this obstacle?
Thinking thus for a moment with a mind becoming despondent, he reflected again:
"[49] This very separation is indeed a treasure for me, who have fallen into impurity. For instance—"
Where there may be a stain caused by an unavoidable matter, a person born of noble family should keep far away from it; this is proper.
For such a stain might be effaced by time, and indeed, in that case, a remedy exists.
Therefore, separation from my herd would result in suffering for me.
Alas! By ill fortune, my affection for my father and others— who are my very life in this cowherd settlement— has been overwhelmed on all sides.
The contraction arises from those very [objects] themselves.
[50] Then he thought again in another way:
"Let the vital breaths abandon the body; let the body also abandon the vital breaths."
But how could those cowherd girls ever mutually renounce their lives for Hari? //GC_2,1.46//
[51] Furthermore, he made even that otherwise:
"In a single dwelling, the separation of husband and wife becomes unbearable."
Therefore, going far leads to the necessity of going at the appointed time.

[52] But alas, O bestower of fame upon Vṛṣabhānu and Bhānu! Alas, O you who, from birth itself, have bestowed goodness of mind upon my own mind by being its very essence! Alas, O you who, from childhood onwards, have gladdened all through the festival of the exquisite tenderness of your body, speech, and mind!
Alas, O you whose thirst is intensified by the spreading flames of the contemplation of separation from me!
Alas, O beloved, consumed by sorrow as you somehow manage to join with me for a moment and then repeatedly part from me, having no other recourse!
Alas, my dear one!
O beloved, now that I— who was once so trusting— am wishing to abandon you through my wicked cruelty, how will you live? Alas, O you who are superior to all happiness!
"O Rādhikā!
Where will you go, here or there?
Then Madhumangala, having approached, reported this unpleasant matter:
They all concluded that Rādhā and the others would remain in perpetual seclusion,
because they were householders.
“They are blocking these does on all sides.

Thus, being unable to pass the time through contemplation that was never-ending and insatiable, nor through the practice of imagining the acquisition of those deer, Kṛṣṇa— his purpose faltering, full of longing, and accompanied by his peers— [remained there].
"Thus, while sporting, he brought the three watches of the night to an end"—enough of this excessive detail that pierces the very vitals of the heart.
Having said this, the narrator states the conclusion:
"O Rādhā, what you have said may not be proper, yet it is also released by those who are liberated."
I endeavored to express clearly the weight of their mutual love.
O Murāri, long ago this story was told by you, which increases passion;
see now, this very lord of my life desires your favor.

[56] Thus, perceiving the manifestation of their pastimes exactly as described, and now finding confidence and solace in the fact that those pastimes have ceased, everyone returned joyfully to their respective homes by way of Mount Govardhana. Śrī Rādhā and Mādhava, however, entered their own bedchamber with a longing full of bliss.
Thus ends the first supplement, titled "The Expansion of the Ocean of Devotion to Vraja," from the glorious and illustrious *Gopālacampū*. 1.
Now follows the second fulfillment:
the fulfillment of Akrūra’s cruelty.
[1] Then, on the following day, as the dawn was shining brightly, there was a conversation in the assembly of the King of Vraja and his circle of princes within the settlement of Vraja, as follows:

[2] Madhukaṇṭha said: Then, on the preceding night, when the slaughter of Keśin had occurred and the dawn had become beautiful, that lotus-eyed one, due to his flickering gaze, reflected for a few moments as follows:
[3] "Aha! This was indeed a dream."
Where Kaṃsa was seen by me as if drawn away from his bed after he had fallen from it— that very place is now close at hand;
for today or tomorrow, Keśin, being intent upon me, will become a neighbor to Yama.
Immediately following that, the destruction of Kaṃsa is indeed the relevant topic.
Once that is the subject at hand, my departure to Nigama is justified by the exigency of the occasion and is supported by sound reasoning;
for surely, the journey of one who is terrified of me cannot here be considered a fit object of reason.

And even now, as long as he continues his incessant threats against the Vṛṣṇis and his constant refusal to dismiss wicked people toward me, both families here and there—my father’s and my own—will remain agitated by fear unless his destruction occurs.
Then he thought again: "Alas!"
Alas!

If there is such a long delay due to the sequence of duties, then I consider it no auspicious omen for the union of our bodies here, even at the cost of my very life and the like. And so, [I shall depart].

If I, who am the moon to my mother’s *cakora*-like eyes, the rain-cloud to my father’s line of *cātaka* birds, and the sun to the lotus-eyes of the people of other cowherd settlements—were I to abandon them and depart, alas! oh! what a tragedy that would be!
Just as it was for the triad beginning with Candra, so shall it be for me; fie upon this whirling of the wheel of wind!

[5] Thus, while she was thus lamenting for a long time upon her bed, O lotus-eyed one, Keśin suddenly became his companion; and his untying reached its conclusion through the very narrative that had first bound them together. [6] Then the beloved of the illustrious Gopeśvarī, whose fame was protected under the guise of his being fanned by white whisks, attained a state of intimate familiarity with the Sage of the Abode of the Thirty-three.
And there, the Sage consoled him— who was possessed of a pride consisting of an excess of latent doubts— by means of his manifest, future divine play.

Then Śrī Gopāla, the protector of all who are worthy of praise, having dismissed him, departed for the cowherd settlement together with his friends and Rāma, despite the distress of his mind being deeply engaged [with the task], because he manifested the splendor of all external happiness upon his face and because of his delight in the company of his friends.
He came to Vraja,
being honored by the gods with garlands of celestial flowers and praised by the hymns of the assemblies of Brahmā through the pathways of heaven.
Everyone beheld him as he appeared, creating before them, by means of his names, both the sacrificial animals and their guardians, and by means of his splendors, bestowing happiness.
And here is the speech of the gods:
"Immediately after the rising of the moon, the multitude of night-lotuses blossoms;
the ocean is agitated; and the flock of cakora birds hastens from afar to drink in its luster."

"O cowherds, behold! Due to the sweet sounds of Murāri, they have reached a state of complete exhaustion, yet out of a sense of extreme satisfaction, they run as far as their strength allows. Thus it is said.
And so:
Hari has arrived here after slaying Keśin; He is the light for those who possess joy, the mass of creative power for His servants,
the inner essence within the hearts of those standing as His friends, the shining life-breath in the hearts of His fathers, mothers, and others,
and the very Self of those who dwell within Him.
Whenever he went to his own home, they too, being well-known, would go to their own bodies.
Then his mother embraced him with her own [arms], his father shed tears from his eyes,

and all the others experienced horripilation with their limbs trembling and blossoming; moreover, there was something else at that time which transcended the range of words, even those spoken with a quivering voice.
Having slain Keśin, that Lord returned to the cowherd settlement of Vraja, which was filled with a tumultuous clamor.

[9] Then, in the morning, their parents— distraught by the incomparable calamity and having ceased their usual abundant fondling and caressing— embraced their son all around and allowed him to rest for a few moments by means of providing him with food, drink, bathing, divine garments, fine perfumes, ointments, and unguents, out of affection for his departure from home.
[10] Because they had always perceived him as being indeed tender, yet at times such as the onset of battle, he became composed of the power manifested by Nārāyaṇa.

[11] Then, thinking that it would be time to descend for the milking of the cows, the venerable Gopāla, the protector of all happiness, joined with his elder brother and, having summoned the multitude of servants who handled his equipment, arrived at the foremost part of their ground.
And as soon as he arrived there, his body dark like that of Rāma, he—
whose roar of the syllable *huṃ* robbed all other sounds of their existence, who possessed the splendor of a fresh rain-cloud, and who had spread out a multitude of cows— [was seen].
Though the calves were absent, this powerful bull, being deeply affectionate toward them, made the milk flow copiously and turned it into curdled whey.
There, Hari performed everything as before; yet,
because of the words of the celestial sage, he held within his heart a deep sorrow.
Even though that [was] so, his resolve to return to his own Vraja took root and grew firm within his heart.
For instance:

"The love for my father's face impels me to set out to kill Kaṃsa; yet the word of the celestial sage, which appears as an obstacle to that, cannot be false. Alas! How then shall I endure separation from Vraja?"

Even when this has been determined, enough with this stain of anxiety consisting of misery; rather, one should constantly remember that glorious majesty full of happiness which will arise here from future association.
Thus he thought, and he beheld a certain chariot;
for the reflection within the hearts of the great indeed attains the status of a reality.
[13] But upon seeing the man standing on the chariot, Kṛṣṇa reasoned that he must be a messenger who had come from Kaṃsa without weapons; others also suspected for what reason he had come from Kaṃsa.

And at that time, the Lord of Day, enamored with the western quarter and intent on setting, having boiled the waters of the Lord of Rivers, caused both his own light and the world to enter into darkness.
Truly, the sun reached the end of the fourth watch; however—
The powerful sun rendered his own rays greenish-yellow, having dispelled the darkness.

[15] Then, when the cowherd folk had turned their faces upward and the herds of cows had simultaneously raised their ears, Balarāma and Kṛṣṇa, standing in the chariot and longing to behold him, recognized him from afar even without prior acquaintance; for:
The view of the wise is that the eye alone serves as the perceiver of mere form; however,
in the experience of such [objects], the ears [are likewise involved].
Even the power of vision undergoes attraction.
Let alone the exquisite beauty of these two, which captivates the splendor of the blue gem and the moon;
even the mark upon their feet is like a wondrous painting.
Even from afar, they repeatedly bewildered him.

[16] He also observed their forms to be such that one was an incarnation of the presiding deity of the beloved wealth of those with dark luster, while alongside him was the expansion of the essence of the delightful abundance arising from a mass of brilliant splendor.

In that regard, its beginning is the manifestation of the Goddess’s splendor drawn forth by the accumulation of the luster of garments; moreover, it is a lovely dwelling that imitates what was created before through the variegation of its radiance.
Likewise—
the first [of the two] bestows joy through the great splendor of his face, which triumphs over the beauty of the blue lotus;
while the delight of the radiance of the second’s face eclipses the familiar luster of the white lotus.
Therein, the first [beauty] is that which illuminates the lovely wagtail created by the splendor of the eyes;
moreover, the other is the goad of the swarm of bees, tawny with the pollen of the reddish flowers within the eyes.
Likewise:
the first [face] has cheeks that provide pleasure to the fish-like mouths within the auspicious earrings,
and its ears possess the splendor of lotus-buds shining with the rays of the single ear-ornament.
Among them, the first was one whose eyebrows were like bows, who possessed a tilaka-flower on his forehead, and whose complexion was like that of an arrow;
moreover, he surpassed the mind of the radiant Kāma by means of the splendor of his second [eye].
Likewise—
the first [pillar] is variegated with gems shining like the serpent-like arms of the Lord of the Nāthas;
that which is adjacent to it is made of rubies and other jewels, its wonderful arms surpassing the pillars.
Among them, the first is the one purified by the golden streaks upon the touchstone of the glorious dark-blue complexion;
and another is the one who, by the luster of his chest, acts as a sieve for the wealth of the splendor of the gems of the earth of Śiva’s mountain.
Likewise—
the first [of these] is endowed with inexhaustible wealth that increases the splendor of the primary, secondary, and minor limbs of poetry;
it is as beautiful at every moment as that very [first], and is so described by all the learned.
There, the first [of the two] was set down by the two lotus-like feet, as if for his own excellent army;
moreover, the other was set down in fear, moving his own feet as if they were assistants to that [first one].
Likewise—
the first [child], whose play was rendered excellent by his hands being like fresh, dark, and supple tree-vines, found a companion for his ball in a branch that had been turned into a plowshare.
"In that regard, the first [type of person] is one whose intellect is constricted, who has obtained a garment for the sake of covering the collection of his limbs;
and what other [type] is there? One who likewise observes the approaching time for the purpose of performing the act of meeting.
And furthermore:
Cool, with garments of lightning, with beautiful earrings always adorning their left ears,
possessing the daughter Rohiṇī who is the source of great splendor, accompanied by the one named Bala,
with cows that yield milk at will for sport, and having abandoned the abodes of other births.
He beheld Balarāma and Keśava between the calves like two young elephants.
Moreover—
clad in garments the color of dark-blue gems and gold, with a pair of spotless horn-flutes fastened at his waist;
With her hand holding a sharp copper staff and a pestle,
Musalī-Harī captivated his heart.

[17] And from the mere sight of him, his journey toward the fruit of immovability having begun, he suddenly descended from the chariot with all its trappings, his limbs bristling with horripilation like a vessel filled with trembling.
[18] Having descended, with his limbs scattered about, he prostrated himself with his entire body;
and because it was limited to that very extent, he rested.
But when she was beaten by her own paternal uncle, he wandered about; for:
"The power that one experiences is caused by one's own previous power;
everything appears differently and differently according to its relative weight or lightness. (GC 2.22)

[19] Thus, as he was intent on uninterrupted prostration, Kṛṣṇa, pointing out that more cows should be milked along with their calves and led to his house, spoke with such an abundance of compassion that, despite the confusion of his own great respect, he assisted Saṅkarṣaṇa; and he, whose frame was like that of a lion, helped him up from the ground with both hands as he rose.
[20] But he, with a faltering voice, was unable to utter his own name.
[21] Then, while the flocks of aged animals were being gathered and the preparations for that [sacrifice] were being made, the two of them became distressed and agitated by that activity.
The two brothers, even forgetting the formalities of uncle and nephew, received him with embraces; each grasping him with his own hand, they led him back to their very home.
Hari, however, conducting himself with proper decorum, made his elder brother alone the leader there.

Then, having extended the first portion of hospitality consisting of a welcome and other courtesies according to the truth, he, together with his younger brother, offered to him a multitude of foods composed of the essence of flavor.
He massaged him;
and when he had finished eating, he joyfully offered him mouth-freshener, which was like breath-fragrance for the mouth.
Immediately thereafter, he caused him to partake of the glorious King of Vraja.
And there, meeting Akrūra as he bowed down, the Lord of Vraja— remembering the sorrow born of Kaṃsa—
honored him with tearful words of blessing, praising him with whatever qualities could remove all his exhaustion.
Even though his nature is so simple, remembering that cruelty of his mind,
my heart trembles, it burns fiercely, and alas, today it turns to ashes.

[24] Then, after he had assigned a dwelling for rest and was seated cross-legged, filled with happiness due to the honor shown to him, Kṛṣṇa himself— having sat down in private with Akrūra, who was joined by those two who had prepared food for their mother, and whose desire to slay Kaṃsa and others had been awakened by that sight—
asked him about this desired matter.
And where this skill in sequential narration, through its sweetness, carries the burden of all happiness:
"O dear father, gentle one, has happiness arrived? Is there well-being for you? Has that wretched Kaṃsa finally been slain?"
Are your parents still living, or what was the auspicious cause for your arrival here?

[25] Then Akrūra said: "Indeed, your persistent enmity toward those Yādava heroes has already been well-established by you; moreover, that enmity which began with my presence at Devakī’s wedding remains vividly in your memory.
As for someone like me, however, I am there like a clump of grass with a hundred joints upon its path."

The son of Devabhaga, the uterine brother of Vasudeva, who is supremely pure and named Uddhava, is also afflicted by the disease of separation from you; because he is afflicted by this wind-like [agitation], he is called Pavanavyadhi, and thus he remains as if left behind.
[26] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "This too is known. But now, tell me what is currently happening, along with its remedy."

[27] But Akrūra, looking all around, spoke these subtle words: "Now, O Śrī Nārada, you are an autumnal season for the joy of victory for one such as I, yet a bridge for crossing over a miserable birth for one such as he. Out of fear for him who is covered by love for Vraja and unstrewn with fear, you have indicated to Devakī that we two shall become her seventh and eighth embryos, as if to incite her desire to fight, though it was inappropriate."

[28] At the outset, indeed, through his power of illusion (māyā), the embryo of Devakī was transferred into Rohiṇī; then, Śrī Vasudeva, perceiving that very same illusion to have attained birth in Yaśodā, placed you— who had been born from Devakī— upon her bed and caused her [the illusion] to attain birth in her [Yaśodā].
[29] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "This appears like a marvel to me.
[30] Akrūra said: "Even from the mouth of the illustrious Ānakadundubhi, my two ears had not become satisfied; now, by this [speech], they have been made fruitful.

[31] Then Śrī Kṛṣṇa, looking for a moment as if embarrassed, suddenly attained this thought within himself: "Ah! Ah! This is due to the power of my immersion in affection for Vraja, even though my knowledge is unimpaired."
Previously it had been manifest before him, but now, like one who has forgotten a dream, he experienced its manifestation upon receiving the sign:
"Many are the forms and names of your son" (BhP 10.8.15). "And many are the names of your son" (BhP 10.8.14).

Furthermore, they have not reflected upon the group of conclusions established by Garga Muni regarding their illustrious father, the protector of Vraja, that "this son of yours was previously born somewhere as the son of Vasudeva.
For indeed, it was by Māyā— who had obtained residence within the womb of my illustrious mother, the protectress of Vraja— [that this occurred].

"Since my arrival there occurred while I had already attained residence in the heart-lotus along with [Viṣṇu] in His two-armed form— yet they did not realize this because they perceived only the concealment of that four-armed form which arose from the heart of Śrī Devakī— they failed to recognize me.
Be that as it may, since I must follow the path of both unclehood and fatherhood, I must certainly effect their deliverance."
[33] He explained clearly what happened next.

[34] Akrūra said: "Then, having pacified that base man who was intent on killing Vasudeva with gentle words and having caused him to wander away, that sage, the enjoyer of sacrifices, departed as he pleased. When he had gone, Kaṃsa, becoming unrestrained, bound your parents with an iron chain."
[35] Then both brothers, with tears in their eyes, made him hear: "In that case, has your arrival occurred merely for the sake of delivering a message to our parents?
[36] Akrūra said with shame: "No, no!
Rather, they truly endure even their own torment at the hands of Kaṃsa."
Indeed, you two do not hear of their fall;
rather, I myself announce this—
even though you two were born and have attained fitness.
"How can the father's distress cease? Where, then, might a daughter-in-law reside?
[37] Śrī Kṛṣṇa, however, concealing his agitation within his heart, spoke with contempt: "What indeed did Kaṃsa declare?
[38] Akrūra said: "How many praises were there for his declaration?"

The essential meaning, however, culminates in this alone: under the pretext of the festival for the King of Spirits (Bhūtarāja), having summoned his own assembly for assistance and deceived us through wicked counsel, he invited even you two—who possess your own cowherd settlements—through our very agency, just like other subjects, so that you might share in that curiosity; and that is precisely what has occurred.
[39] Rāma said with a laugh: "This is surely the trumpeting of a rutting elephant toward a lion whose hunger has been intensified.
[40] Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Let it be so."
"We too shall come together and, having offered that same oblation (bali), satisfy the Lord of Beings.
But when will we meet those people in the assembly hall of the King of Beings?
[41] Akrūra said: "On the fourteenth day."

[42] Thus, having arranged for the remainder of the special attire as requested, Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "Since this [discourse] is the supreme auspiciousness for us through its very investigation, let us therefore go into the presence of our venerable father.
[43] Having spoken thus and leaving him right there, Rāma rose up and went to his father's side.
Then, after being seated according to that instruction, with his lotus-face gazed upon by him, he joined his palms in reverence and made this clear with his words:
"Father, there is a certain auspicious event;
however, it must be announced to everyone all at once, as if to all the quarters simultaneously."

[44] Then the King of Vraja, his doubts dispelled, joyfully summoned Upananda and the others. There, the queens of Vraja, led by the illustrious Queen of Vraja, were granted the opportunity for private conversation once the formalities of concealment had been somewhat arranged.
When those remaining had sat down comfortably, the illustrious Viṣṭaraśravas (Kṛṣṇa), as if smiling slightly, said: "The King of the Bhojas has now sent this message to us:"
It is so.
O you who resemble progeny, you who are progeny—come here to this great festival of the bow of Maheśa, together with the Lord, together with your offspring, and with space for all.
Especially, however, [come] Rāma and Kṛṣṇa, whose thirst for the sight of their own [Lord] is being stirred by their own prowess.
And so it was said.
Vrajarāja said: "What does your mind think regarding this—that he comes from Vasudeva, and that he feels affection for him?"

[46] Śrī-Kṛṣṇa said with a smile: "Even if it were otherwise, such a desire of yours would still be a pursuit of a futile path. For who indeed could inflict harm upon me, who am endowed with the power of your own majesty? [47] Indeed, even while I was in my childhood, which is naturally devoid of strength, Pūtanā and the others met their end."
How much more so, then, did the desire to seize them arise from mere pleasure for those who were already turning back, as they turned toward the faces of the crane and the calf?
And therein,
the crane was one who swallows with a single gulp, while the other remained a devourer of all limbs.
Among them, Indra is the all-scorcher; as for Kaṃsa, whom does he approach?

[48] Having heard this and having deliberated among themselves, when those [enemies] had been thoroughly struck down by their correct counter-measures, and when Mātṛ and the others had their life-breaths severed by the destruction of their expedition, he spoke again: "For us, who have formed a league with ten million cows (or ten million kine), no opportunity for even a dance is seen against another."

If one departs by transgressing the king's command, there will certainly be fear arising from his pursuit; how much more so if one remains? Therefore, we perceive that our going there without hesitation is itself the means to pacify him.
Having heard this, the illustrious Nanda, turning pale with distress, said to Upananda: "What should be done?
He replied: "One must go there; the child has spoken most correctly.
Indeed, the inability to go would only serve to awaken his anger and his fear."
But destiny drives even that away.
Furthermore, that very thing which was unprecedented, yet had previously provided protection for what was unprecedented, shall now lead even those who are close to crossing through the gateway.
[50] Then, as he was thus employing such reasoning, the full moon of his majesty and presence, filled with power, arrived there with great speed within the circle of cowherds.
[51] Then, when the King of Vraja had asked his question, she spoke with affection: "Upon the departure for Mathurā of your son, there shall be universal joy;
Kaṃsa and all others who are cruel will meet their destruction.
However, we observe a delay in his arrival at Vraja, so please decide what is appropriate."
Upananda said: "Even arriving without delay is indeed better, provided it results in the subduing of our enemies; therefore, going itself is preferable and more delightful.

Then, all of them, having concluded that there was no other course of action and that this was the appropriate thing to say, spoke without any further lamentation, looking toward the glorious face of Śrī Kṛṣṇa and making Him the subject of their inquiry.
In that regard, when should it be considered that they must go?
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "We shall see their departure on the morning of the thirteenth day, brought about by the power of yoga;
indeed, on the fourteenth day, that great festival will attain its full magnificence."

[54] Thus, while he was lamenting within himself, "I alone am seen here as the god among men of Vraja," everyone said, echoing the cry of the entire community: "Let it be arranged immediately so that the cowherds may come to the royal assembly with their offerings this very morning. [55] Then the illustrious King Nanda addressed the assembly: "O noble-minded ones, according to your view, everything will surely turn out auspiciously; therefore, let what is beneficial be ordained."
"In every direction, let the cowherds bring offerings as gifts.
Having thus obtained their consent, the Lord of Vṛndāvana commanded his own attendants: "Let this message be told to Kṣattṛ.

Madhukaṇṭha, speaking thus, had his throat choked with emotion, for the Queen of Vraja, having learned this, was rendered unconscious by delusion and was unable to say or do anything at all. And he remained likewise.
It was exactly so.

Then, while that same confusion persisted even in the assembly during the discourse, the Crown Prince of Vraja, simultaneously grasping the pair of lotus-feet of the King of Vraja in that very gathering, spoke to him once more as he restored him to life: "O Father!"
Why do you act so timidly?
This is indeed merely a story as it was before;
however, I, this very person, having subdued Kaṃsa through the delight of meditating upon you, have returned after a long time and am now following within the path of your vision.
[59] Then, while the King of Vraja protected his lap—which was covered with horripilation—everyone spoke with immense pride of joy as the story reached its peaceful conclusion. Madhukaṇṭha said:
"O Lord of Vraja, where else could your son find delight except in you?
Behold, he who is filled with compassion for his devotees is truly under your control."

[60] Then, while the splendor created by Śrī Kṛṣṇa was present and the assembly of Rādhā was gathered for a night-discourse, Madhukaṇṭha spoke with a faltering voice: "O Śrī Rādhā, whose affliction of separation has now been removed by Śrī Mādhava!
Please listen to what occurred in the past."
Then he suddenly experienced a roar, powerful like a thunderclap,
by which the other [sounds] were instantly struck down.
And Rādhikā and the others are as if struck down with grief.
[61] This being so—some had their faces withered by the flame born from the fire of hearing that;
some had their limbs emaciated, their garments hanging loose, and their bodies resembling inert matter; and some were deprived of their senses.

By what means can these [states] be described? For here, one who has experienced the pain of that state within his own heart, or one who is devoid of contact with it—both of them alike fall into utter insensibility.
Then, that very proclamation which at night brought about the fainting of the women, produced at dawn the awakening of consciousness;
for when the body is scorched by fire, heat itself serves as the remedy for that heat.
Even poison is considered the best remedy for one corrupted by poison; this is the consensus of physicians.

And for those who had regained consciousness, although there was no longer any fear of the bronze vessel, a certain other protection— conceived through the power of their present state of being, as if fashioned by a deity to guard them against the imminent danger— manifested in their minds, having been firmly resolved upon by Pūrṇamāsī.
In that place where the serpent Kāliya, the son of Kadru, as well as Keśin and the bull Ariṣṭa were destroyed,
Kaṃsa would surely have died.

"Not even a trace of doubt appears there. (2.31) Thus it was said. Therefore, having thus considered that which is universally accepted by the world, he reflected once more on the victory over Kaṃsa achieved by the enemy of Bakī (Kṛṣṇa).
We fear the destruction of our own interests:
how could he, who might be king in the royal capital of the Yadavas, remain here in a cow-pen?
"We are village girls here, daughters of cowherds; the city maidens are princesses living in the town. But Kṛṣṇa’s mind is captivated by virtues; therefore—"
How could we possibly have any recollection of its interior? //GC_2.2.33//
A single blink of an eye would be an eon for him, in whose forest-dwelling even the passing of time is such a hardship that neither he himself nor anyone else can perceive it;
yet his departure from the city of Mathurā for the sake of the kingdom is this very thing.
How then, alas, can even a modicum of fortitude be maintained by us? //GC_2.2.34//
Alas, this birth of passion in us craves nothing else; it finds no peace even in his kingdom, but desires only to serve him in solitude, for our very selves—
like fish fearing separation from the nectar of his glance— long for him with our inner thoughts as our dearest life-breath.
Therefore, while still drying up even before that time, he does not reckon anything here—neither the beyond nor the further.

Alas! Having directly perceived his face, beautiful with its smile, his eyes with their playful side-glances, the playfulness of his speech which bestows joy upon the mind, and his world-enchanting graceful movements—
how could that thought of obstacles ever have tolerated even a comparison with them?
If she could endure the pain of renunciation, she would not perceive poison there as nectar.

[64] Thus, overcome with anxiety and free from any suspicion of blemish, they all rushed forward to behold Śyāmagātra, who had set out on his journey for their sake. As for the arrangements for the procession, it would depart at dawn.
[65] Having said this, Madhukaṇṭha fell into a state of paralysis due to the failure of his resolve; meanwhile, Mādhava, observing that Rādhā was suffering from an emerging faint, quickly—
He spoke again:
"O Rādhā, this is but an old story; it is not the present situation.
Behold, even he who used to wither away upon seeing your face now withers away."

[66] Thus, having served the very essence of union like food for one who is hungry at the conclusion of that [discourse], and having gratified everyone with ease, the pair of narrators returned to their own abode,
as did Śrī Rādhā and Mādhava to their own enchanting palace.
Thus ends the *Śrī-śrīmad Uttara-gopāla-campū*.
The second fulfillment, named "The Fulfillment of Akrūra’s Cruelty," is concluded.
Now begins the third fulfillment.

The Departure for the City of Śrī Mathurā [1]. Now, during a morning discourse in the assembly of the King of Vraja, which took place on a day of auspicious deeds performed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa, Snigdhakaṇṭha said: "O King of Vraja!"
Shining with the splendor of King Śrī Hari’s face,
we shall once again illuminate this history.
Now, when only a very small portion of the night remained, and even the measure of the journey was but a mere vesselful for one whose body was emaciated, by the brother of Rāma—
The strings of virudas composed by the authors of hymns, being powerfully connected with the deeds such as the slaying of Pūtanā,
brought about a presentation that inspired everyone with pride;
let alone the news of others.
Wherein His parents, considering even the destruction of Kaṃsa to have been accomplished, were delighted and bestowed great wealth upon the bards;
[there] She attained the state of the wife of the Lord of Vraja.
Rohiṇī is not described separately here;
for those who speak of the beauty of the reflection necessarily describe the original object itself.

[3] Then, at the auspicious hour of departure, while the musical ensemble had begun and the two Lords of Vraja were once again absorbed in the intensity of their deliberations and preparations, experts in astrology and those possessing the excellence of knowledge regarding omens gathered at the gate and, through the medium of charming attendants, informed them of their own impending journey.

[4] Immediately thereafter, having stationed those very persons without interval within the inner apartments themselves, and having at that time administered an oath with their hands holding vessels containing the customary gifts, he questioned them in secret: "What do you perceive, you who have experienced everything?"
[5] They said: "Why is this matter of extreme happiness being asked about in private?
This should be celebrated in the presence of everyone. For instance:
'O lords of the Vraja land, do not fear; your son is clearly [the Lord] himself.'"
Having brought about the destruction of Kaṃsa, he will become the lord of the fortune of the three worlds;
by him the three worlds shall forever have their faces made to dance by the multitude of his glories,
and the Veda, together with the Pañcamaveda and the Tantras, shall serve as witness here.
[6] Then, having inflicted many hardships and afflictions upon them and keeping them in his heart,
